population.note: FICTIONAL. ~265M US adults; 15.2% current is about 40.3M people on an incretin for any reason; 21% ever is about 55.7M. Cycling arithmetic: ever 21 minus current 15.2 leaves 5.8 pp who used before and are off now. About 4.5 pp of current users are restarters (≈30% of current, consistent with 36–47% of stoppers restarting within a year), and about 1.8 pp of the off-now group have cycled at least once before. (4.5+1.8)/21 gives 30% of ever-users who have cycled. Payer mix of the ~40.3M: ~15M diabetes-coded (still broadly covered); ~8M commercial obesity coverage; ~2.6M Medicare Bridge obesity; ~1.1M Medicaid obesity (14 opt-in states); ~11M cash through manufacturer, TrumpRx or telehealth channels (of which ~3.5M are 'metabolic health' users with BMI<27 and no diabetes); ~2.5M compounded or imported. Total 40.2M. 65+: 13% of ~62M is about 8M (≈5M diabetes Part D + 2.6M Bridge + ~0.4M cash). Income thirds average (20.5+14.5+10.6)/3 = 15.2. The middle third gained least because employer retreat hit it hardest while the bottom gained through Medicaid and LIS. The age bands, weighted by population shares (20/33/24/23%), give about 15.2%. Pediatric: about 0.8% of under-18s (~580k), mostly 12–17; under-12 use is still off-label and specialist-only. Never-able-to-afford: an estimated 22–26M adults with obesity in non-opt-in Medicaid states or employer plans that dropped coverage have never filled a prescription.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge converted (Nov 2027) into a standing CMMI model through Dec 2030: Medicare still pays $245/month and beneficiary copay stays $50, cut to $0 for Part D Low-Income Subsidy enrollees. About 2.6M obesity-indicated users: 2.6M × $245 × 12 ≈ $7.6B/yr, plus ~0.6M LIS users × $50 × 12 ≈ $0.36B/yr for the waived copays, ≈ $8.0B/yr. Medicaid: 14 states opted in at the same $245. ~1.1M enrollees × $245 × 12 ≈ $3.2B/yr total, federal share at ~65% ≈ $2.1B/yr. Federal run-rate for obesity indications ≈ $10B/yr, which puts the CBO's ≥$35B 2026–2034 score on track to be exceeded before 2031. Several large states (incl. California and Pennsylvania) still exclude obesity coverage in Medicaid.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 60+ generic semaglutide brands at ~$6–40/month. Canada: generics ~CAD 70–100/month, and the main source of personal-importation mail orders to the US. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and much of Southeast Asia have generics. Generic semaglutide is available in ~165 countries.
access.note: Shock up: after the 2027 fill-finish failure, Novo suspended discounted injectable cash offers for new patients. TrumpRx Wegovy pens stayed at $349 instead of falling to the planned $245. Lilly raised Zepbound vial cash prices from $349–499 to $399–549 in Jan 2028, citing demand. Wegovy list rose to $1,399. Oral entry doses held at $149 (Foundayo, Wegovy pill), but maintenance oral doses run $299–399. Semaglutide injection was on the FDA shortage list from Apr 2027 to Feb 2028, which reopened 503A compounding legally for ten months. The 503B exclusion was finalised in 2027. Compounded and imported product reached ~2.5M users (~6% of users). Orals are ~40% of new starts and ~30% of all users. Employer coverage for weight management is 44% (Business Group on Health, 2028), down from 60%. Where coverage survives it is gated to BMI≥35 or diabetes, cardiovascular, OSA or CKD codes, often requiring 'lifestyle programme' enrolment.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
GLP-1 + amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Dec 2026)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Apr 2028)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (tirzepatide, 2027)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'metabolic health' / longevity use by people with BMI<27 and no diabetes: low-dose oral orforglipron or semaglutide by cash telehealth subscription, ~3.5M users
alcohol reduction: still no approval; Novo filed an sNDA for semaglutide in alcohol use disorder in mid-2028, and addiction clinics prescribe off-label
pediatric under-12 use off-label under specialist care
nicotine and gambling craving reduction: observational evidence only, with heavy telehealth marketing that the FDA polices
drugs.pipeline_note: CagriSema approved Dec 2026, but uptake is modest because it failed non-inferiority against tirzepatide. Retatrutide BLA filed Jan 2027 and approved Apr 2028 (15 months later); its label carries dysesthesia and lists apathy/anhedonia as uncommon. Survodutide filed Jul 2027 and is under review, with a decision no earlier than Jul 2028 that slipped to 2029 after an FDA information request. Amycretin is in phase 3, readout 2028–29, and not filed. Monthly driver honoured with what the rules allow: Amgen filed the MariTide (monthly) BLA in Jun 2028 using a Commissioner's National Priority Voucher, with a decision expected 2029. It is not on the US market. Implantable depots are still phase 2. Muscle-preserving adjuncts (bimagrumab combos) are in phase 2/3. Global incretin market ~$110B in 2028.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of discontinuation. Orals have similar GI profiles at maintenance doses.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis' retained.

safety_ledger.effect: Gastroparesis / persistent delayed gastric emptying and ileus (mass-tort scale)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Delayed gastric emptying on-drug is established pharmacology. Whether it persists after discontinuation is disputed: two 2027 claims-database studies found a small excess (≈1–3 per 1,000 user-years); manufacturers' analyses found none. MDL 3094 (E.D. Pa.) passed ~31,000 filed claims by mid-2028, including pancreatitis and intestinal obstruction claims.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA 2027 safety communication and label strengthening on ileus/obstruction and on perioperative aspiration. First bellwether trials are scheduled for 2028–29. DOJ civil investigative demand to Novo Nordisk after the unsealed pharmacovigilance documents.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss, and higher with the triple agonist.
Long-term RCTs still do not confirm causation; absolute risk is low. It is the second-largest claim category in the MDL.
~25–30% of weight lost is lean mass. Concern now extends to normal-weight 'metabolic' users and to Medicare Bridge enrollees over 75.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No regulatory action. CMS model guidance recommends resistance-training referral. Adjunct drugs are in trials.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohort studies still conflict; a large 2027 pooled analysis estimated a modest relative increase with wide intervals.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA labels it 'very rare'. FDA added it to US semaglutide labels under postmarketing experience in 2027.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association in subsequent analyses.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The FDA's Jan 2026 removal of the warning stands.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, apathy)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Acknowledged as uncommon. Retatrutide's phase 3 safety tables reported apathy/anhedonia in ~0.6% vs 0.2% placebo, and a 2027 pharmacovigilance review gave similar 'uncommon' (0.1–1%) frequencies for the class. Often dose-dependent and reversible on dose reduction.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Listed as 'uncommon' in the retatrutide label (2028) and in EU semaglutide/tirzepatide SmPCs. US class labelling is under FDA review.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Trial and real-world figures still diverge; regain is substantial for most within 1–2 years. The 2027 shortage created a natural experiment of forced stops that is now being analysed.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; it keeps reinforcing the chronic-therapy framing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Signal reproduced in older adults; concern in low-intake normal-weight users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional-society guidance (2027) recommends baseline labs; no label change.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; adolescents on decades-long therapy; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exist. Cycling is common (~30% of ever-users) and unstudied by design.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements attached to CagriSema and retatrutide.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reports climbed again during the 2027 shortage window, passing ~3,400 cumulative FDA adverse-event reports. A counterfeit-pen cluster was seized at the Canadian mail border.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised (2027). A new warning-letter wave followed the shortage's end in Feb 2028. CBP has stepped up its personal-importation enforcement, but it is inconsistent.

safety_ledger.effect: Use in normal-weight people for 'metabolic health' (bone, lean mass, disordered eating)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~3.5M users with BMI<27. Eating-disorder clinics report GLP-1 involvement in a rising minority of adolescent and young-adult intakes. No RCTs exist in this population.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA warning letters on 'longevity' marketing claims; prescribing itself is off-label and legal.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~30% of US households. Packaged-snack and confectionery volumes are down low-to-mid single digits per year, offset by price, protein and portion-packing. 'GLP-1 friendly' is a standard front-of-pack callout, and two major snack makers have divested sweet-baked lines. Grocery calories per GLP-1 household are down ~6–8%.

alcohol.state: Spirits and beer volumes are down further. On-premise is hit hardest among the heavy-drinking decile, and distillers have cut US guidance two years running. Non-alcoholic and low-ABV lines are growing but do not offset the loss. Alcohol lobbyists are quietly opposing the semaglutide AUD sNDA's marketing claims.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat and checks are smaller. Half-portion and 'small plate' menus are standard at casual-dining chains, and fine dining is premiumising further. Dessert and second-drink attachment rates are down.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting, with store closures at Torrid and DXL. Mainstream brands have shifted size curves smaller. Alteration and resale businesses are growing.

fitness.state: Strength-training gyms and 'GLP-1 companion' coaching are growing. Some employers pay for gym-based programmes as the condition for remaining coverage. Cardio-only boutique studios are shrinking.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is down to 44%. Coverage concentrates on diabetes, cardiovascular, OSA and CKD codes, and prior auth plus BMI≥35 gates are standard. Pharmacy trend is moderating at the cost of exclusions. Some carriers sell 'GLP-1 rider' supplemental policies at $60–120/month.

pharma.state: Lilly is the clear leader on orals, tirzepatide and now retatrutide. Novo is wounded by the 2027 fill-finish failure, the unsealed documents and a DOJ inquiry, and its CMO resigned. US prices are rising at the margin while ex-US prices collapse. Amgen is waiting on the monthly MariTide BLA. Litigation reserves are disclosed but small relative to revenue.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: In professional and suburban circles a mid-sized body over 40 is assumed to be medicated. The question has flipped from 'are you on it?' to 'why are you off it?' Accepted answers are pregnancy or trying to conceive, surgery, side effects or cost, and cost is the one people least like to say. The flip is sharpest among women 40–64 in salaried jobs; in the Dallas–Fort Worth suburbs, local surveys put use among them above 30%.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Two tiers have hardened. Salaried and affluent people are on tirzepatide or retatrutide, through surviving coverage or cash. Hourly workers whose employers dropped coverage are on the cheapest oral dose, on cash Canadian imports, or off. Medicare LIS and opt-in Medicaid states have created a third pocket of free access for the poorest, so the visible gap is now the middle third. In Kentucky, a Medicaid opt-in state, Medicaid enrollees are more likely to be on the drug than workers at small firms.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Half-portions are normal and so is sharing a single entrée. 'Food noise' is everyday vocabulary. Holiday and wedding catering budgets have shifted from volume to a few high-intensity bites. Off-drug guests are the ones who finish plates.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating-app bios increasingly state medication status ('on Zep, no judgment'). Couples where one partner is on and one is off report mismatched appetites at meals and, less often, in desire. Fertility clinics now routinely schedule GLP-1 washouts.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a dial rather than a trait. Normal-weight 'metabolic' users frame it as optimisation, alongside continuous glucose monitors and blood panels. Being hungry is beginning to read as a lifestyle choice.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Acknowledged as uncommon, roughly 0.1–1% of users, more with higher-dose triple agonists. Clinics now ask a two-question apathy screen at dose escalation, and dose reduction is standard first-line management. With ~40M users, 'uncommon' still means tens to hundreds of thousands of people.
interior_life.framing: A side effect with a label frequency, like insomnia on a stimulant. Addiction medicine treats the same mechanism as therapy (the AUD sNDA), but the public mostly keeps the two separate: 'the flatness' is a dosing problem, the drinking reduction is a benefit.
interior_life.effect_on_work: No measurable productivity effect at population level. A minority report lost drive and ask for dose reductions. HR departments field occasional accommodation requests citing label-listed apathy. Some sales and hospitality managers note that client dinners and drinks have shortened.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Muted enjoyment is a recognised minority complaint. Music and comedy podcasts joke about 'Zep shows', crowds who stop at one drink. Bar trivia and bowling leagues report lower spending but not lower attendance. A small essay and songwriting genre about 'coming off to feel things' circulates online.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Clinicians address reduced libido and connection as an uncommon, dose-related effect. Couples therapists report on/off appetite mismatch as a more common issue than anhedonia itself.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Politics is about price and payer, not mood. The Canada and India price gap is a stock campaign line, and the Medicare subsidy is popular with seniors. The MDL and the Novo documents feed a bipartisan 'what did they know' hearing. Some fiscal hawks contest the subsidy's cost.

state.regulatory_posture: Still pro-speed on approvals, using priority vouchers for retatrutide and the MariTide filing. Tougher on manufacturing quality after the 2027 consent decree, and on 'longevity' marketing claims, but it does not restrict off-label prescribing. Compounding briefly re-legalised by the shortage listing, then cracked down on again.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Direct subsidy: the Medicare Bridge is now a standing model through 2030 at $245/month, with a $50 copay and $0 for LIS enrollees, plus Medicaid opt-in at the same rate in 14 states. Federal run-rate ≈ $10B/yr (arithmetic in access.public_coverage). There is no mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage is gated by BMI and comorbidity. Some employers require gym or coaching enrolment, tracked through app check-ins. The CMS model requires annual reweighing for renewal. There is no adherence surveillance beyond refill data.
state.workforce_or_military: No mandate. The DoD covers GLP-1s for dependents only under diabetes or cardiac codes. Recruiting commands quietly allow waivers for applicants who lost weight on-drug, provided they are off it for 90 days before accession.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Novo's US fill-finish failure exposed concentration in a handful of sterile-injectable sites. Canada's generics are the main gray-market source into the US, and pressure on Ottawa to restrict export-oriented online pharmacies is growing. India's generics anchor global prices. US exclusivity to ~2031–32 is intact.

events.event: FDA consent decree halts output at a Novo Nordisk US fill-finish site after sterility failures. Semaglutide injection returns to the FDA shortage list in April, and Novo suspends discounted cash pens for new patients. Hundreds of thousands of users are forced off for weeks or switch to compounded product.

Documents unsealed in GLP-1 MDL 3094 show Novo Nordisk pharmacovigilance staff flagged a post-discontinuation gastric-emptying signal in 2020 internal analyses that were never submitted to the FDA. Novo's chief medical officer resigns, the DOJ opens a civil inquiry, and filed claims pass 20,000 by year end and ~31,000 by mid-2028.

CMS converts the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge into a standing model through 2030 at $245/month and waives the $50 copay for Low-Income Subsidy enrollees. Fourteen state Medicaid programmes opt in by mid-2028.

Business Group on Health survey: employers covering weight-management GLP-1s fall to 44% from 60%. Most survivors restrict coverage to BMI≥35 or diabetes and cardiac codes. Lilly raises Zepbound vial cash prices by $50 a month.

FDA approves Lilly's retatrutide for obesity, with labels for dysesthesia and for apathy/anhedonia as 'uncommon'. The same month, three telehealth platforms report a combined ~3.5M cash subscribers to low-dose 'metabolic health' oral GLP-1 plans, most without obesity.
Amgen files a BLA for MariTide, a once-monthly injectable, under a National Priority Voucher, with an FDA decision expected in 2029. Employers already ask about monthly dosing as an adherence fix.

open_tensions: The federal subsidy is running at ~$10B/yr while employers retreat. Public money now pays for the poorest and the old, the middle third pays cash or goes without, and the CBO score is visibly breaking.
MDL bellwether trials and the DOJ inquiry into Novo will set the price of the GI/pancreatic signal just as retatrutide and a monthly MariTide push more people onto stronger, longer-acting drugs.
About 3.5M normal-weight people take low-dose GLP-1s for 'metabolic health' with no trial evidence. Eating-disorder clinics see the edge of it, and regulators police only the marketing.
The forced stops of 2027 and routine cycling (~30% of ever-users) are generating the first large natural experiment on what on/off use does, and the answers will arrive inside the next window.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US; exclusivity runs to roughly 2031–32.
Medicare pays $245/month for obesity GLP-1s with a standard $50 beneficiary copay (now waived only for LIS enrollees).
Oral initial doses (Foundayo/orforglipron and Wegovy pill) are still priced at $149 cash via TrumpRx and manufacturer channels.
Indian generic semaglutide sells for roughly single- to double-digit dollars a month across dozens of brands.
The FDA's January 2026 removal of the suicidal-ideation warning from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels stands; the effect remains debunked.

prose.headline: Why Are You Off It? 40 Million Americans Are on GLP-1s, Uncle Sam Pays for Grandma, and Everyone Else Pays Cash
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 about one American adult in seven is taking an incretin drug, and in the offices and cul-de-sacs where the drugs first spread, nobody remarks on it. The question people get asked is why they stopped. Pregnancy is a good answer and surgery is acceptable. Cost is the honest answer for millions, and the one they least like to give.

The money moved in two directions at once. Employers kept retreating: fewer than half now cover weight-management prescriptions, and those that do want a BMI of 35 or a diabetes or cardiac code, often with a gym check-in app attached. Washington went the other way. In November 2027 CMS made the Medicare Bridge pilot a standing model through 2030, still at $245 a month, and waived the $50 copay for the poorest seniors. Fourteen state Medicaid programmes joined at the same price. The federal bill for obesity coverage is now about ten billion dollars a year, so the old budget score looks quaint. The result is an access map shaped like an hourglass. The old and the poor are covered, the affluent pay for the best drugs, and the hourly middle juggles a $149 starter pill, Canadian mail-order pens and gaps.

Prices did not fall the way they were supposed to. In March 2027 an FDA consent decree shut a Novo Nordisk fill-finish plant, and semaglutide pens went back on the shortage list. For ten months compounders were legal again, and the gray market that regulators had nearly strangled came back to a few million users. Novo pulled its cheap cash offers. Lilly, holding the field, raised its vial prices by fifty dollars. The entry-dose orals stayed at $149, but nobody stays on the entry dose.

The drugs got stronger. Lilly's retatrutide was approved in April with mean weight loss near 28 percent. Its label says what clinics had been saying for two years: apathy and reduced pleasure are uncommon, dose-related and usually reversible. Most doctors now ask two questions about motivation at each dose step, and most patients answer no to both. Amgen has filed for a once-monthly shot. Employers are already asking whether a monthly drug would make them less nervous about paying for one people quit.

The ledger got heavier too. In a Philadelphia federal courtroom the gastroparesis and pancreatitis litigation grew past thirty thousand claims. In September 2027 unsealed documents showed Novo safety staff had seen a gastric-emptying signal in internal analyses that never reached the FDA. A chief medical officer resigned, the Justice Department opened an inquiry and Congress held a hearing. Prescriptions did not slow, and bellwether trials begin next year.

The newest users are not heavy. About three and a half million people with ordinary BMIs take low-dose pills by telehealth subscription for what the apps call metabolic health. They sit alongside continuous glucose monitors and quarterly blood panels. No trial has studied them. Eating-disorder clinics have started asking new patients which subscription they use.

The culture has absorbed all this. Casual-dining chains print half-portion menus, wedding caterers sell five intense bites instead of a buffet, and distillers keep cutting their guidance. Plus-size chains keep closing stores while alteration shops multiply. Dating profiles state medication status the way they once stated smoking. The tension that comes up most in therapy is not flatness. It is one spouse on and one off, eating different dinners at the same table.

In India the same molecule costs less than a streaming subscription, and in Canada less than a tank of gas. Politicians of both parties say so often.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marcus Bell clocks in at the HVAC dispatch office in Columbus at 6:40 and takes his Foundayo dry, the way he used to take nothing. It's the 24-milligram dose now, $399 a month on his own card since January, when the company letter said weight management was no longer a covered benefit and thanked him for his understanding.

At nine Teresa from billing brings in a box of bakery cookies for her birthday. By noon there are eleven left. Somebody jokes that Marcus should take three, since he's the one who can still eat, and he laughs a beat late.

At lunch he calls his mother in Lexington. Her Zepbound came yesterday and the pharmacy charged her nothing, which she still finds suspicious. "They asked me to stand on a scale for the renewal," she says. "Like a prize hog."

His wife Dana texts a photo of her blood panel from the app. Her number is good. She's a size six and takes the little pill anyway, $129 a month. She says it makes her quieter inside.

In the afternoon a customer in Grove City wants a tech who 'isn't on anything', because the last one forgot the filter. Marcus logs the request without comment.

At home Dana has made salmon, two small pieces. Their son Eli, fourteen and broad-shouldered, eats three helpings of rice and looks at his parents' plates like they're a rumor.

After dinner Marcus opens the Canadian pharmacy site in one tab and his bank balance in another, and closes both.
